1	---
2	name: design-taste-frontend
3	description: >-
4	  tasteskill v2, the anti-slop frontend skill. Art direction for websites, distilled from a study of
5	  247 curated gallery sites (One Page Love, Awwwards Sites of the Day). Deals researched directions
6	  (idea, composition, type, palette, photographs, section blueprints) from a library, enforces a strict
7	  no-slop house style with a real-browser inspector, and runs a look-and-fix loop on screenshots. Use
8	  this whenever you build, design, redesign, restyle, polish or review a landing page, marketing site,
9	  portfolio, product page, one-pager, hero or any public-facing web page, in any stack (HTML/CSS, React,
10	  Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind) — also when the user says a page looks generic, templated,
11	  "AI-made", sloppy, or asks to make it look designed, premium, award-level or less like every other
12	  site. Also for app screens: dashboards, admin and analytics views, settings, inboxes and other screens
13	  people work in, with their own run and rules.
14	---
15	
16	# tasteskill v2
17	
18	A page built by a model usually looks like the average of every page the model has seen: a centred
19	headline over three lines, a little label above it, a row of icon cards, a soft gradient, a few thin
20	rules and a monospace caption. Nothing in it is wrong and nothing in it was decided.
21	
22	This skill replaces those defaults with decisions, in four ways:
23	
24	1. **A script deals the directions, you choose among them.** Asked to invent a look, a model picks
25	   the category default every time. `scripts/draw.mjs` deals three of twenty researched directions;
26	   you choose the one that carries the subject's idea, and the script then deals its type system,
27	   palette, hero and section compositions from a library distilled from 247 real sites.
28	2. **The idea comes from the subject.** In the study, what separated the best sites from the forgettable
29	   ones was a concept taken from the thing itself, not the styling.
30	3. **A house style with no ornaments,** measured in a real browser by `scripts/inspect.mjs`, so the
31	   rules are checked rather than hoped for.
32	4. **You look at what you made.** Screenshots at three widths, a juror's rubric, fix, look again.
33	
34	One warning learned in testing. Taking the ornaments away is only half the job; a page that has lost its
35	labels, rules and cards and gained nothing in their place reads as thin, and blind jurors rightly prefer
36	a richer page with tells over an empty page without them. The other half is substance: type set
37	larger, whole fields of colour, real pictures of this subject's world (found or drawn), and every
38	section carrying its full content. The skill is built to give you that; do not trade it for restraint.
39	
40	In the commands below `<skill>` is this skill's folder. Run them from the project's root, so the
41	working files land in `.taste-skill/` there. The scripts need Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge
42	or Chromium, and install nothing. `assets.mjs` also needs network access; it uses no API keys.
43	
44	## Page or app screen
45	
46	Decide first which of two kinds of work this is.
47	
48	- **A page** is read and scrolled: a landing page, a marketing or product site, a portfolio, an
49	  event, a restaurant, a one-pager. It follows **the run** below.
50	- **An app screen** is worked in: a dashboard, an admin or analytics view, settings, billing, an inbox
51	  or queue to work through, a wallet, a list with filters, an editor or builder. It follows
52	  **`references/app-screens.md`**: its own run, its own draw (`draw.mjs --app`), its own house rules
53	  (quiet borders, small labels and repeated panels are normal there; gradients, glows, icons in tinted
54	  squares, rainbow charts and invented vanity numbers are not) and `inspect.mjs --app`. Read that file
55	  whole before you start; the page run below does not apply.
56	
57	A product site that shows its app is a page; the interface fragments on it follow the app-screen
58	rules for their insides. Deal the product's app style once, in its own folder, with the page's colours
59	and type kept:
60	
61	```bash
62	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --app --kind <kind> --brief "<the product>" --keep palette,type --out .taste-skill/app
63	```
64	
65	and build every fragment the page shows (the hero's live screen, a feature's crop, a chart) as a real
66	piece of that app: `assets/app.css` for its panels, tables and controls, `assets/charts.js` for its
67	charts, real data that adds up, one finding stated, cropped and scaled the way the page's blueprint
68	treats a picture. A fragment that looks like a working product is the strongest picture a software page
69	has; grey bars and lorem numbers are the weakest. When a request mixes both (a landing page and the
70	dashboard behind it), build each with its own run and one shared palette and typeface.
71	
72	## The run
73	
74	Do these in order. Steps 1–5 take a few minutes and decide whether the page is any good.
75	
76	### 1. Read the brief and the project
77	
78	Find out what is real: the subject, the audience, the one thing the page must get someone to do, the
79	stack, any existing brand (colours, fonts, logo), and above all **what imagery truly exists**: the
80	project's own photographs or product shots, a real interface that can be shown, an image generation
81	tool you can call, or nothing. Do not plan around pictures you do not have. Nothing of its own is
82	rarely nothing at all: the subject's city, street, materials and history are in open archives and
83	museums, free to use with a credit (step 6, `scripts/assets.mjs`).
84	
85	If the request is vague, decide and state your reading in one line instead of asking. Ask only when a
86	missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name).
87	
88	Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to
89	no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and
90	neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop
91	fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the
92	price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by
93	appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at
94	seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where
95	the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on
96	such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that
97	makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list
98	is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6.
99	
100	### 2. Write the argument
101	
102	Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way
103	`references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any
104	section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features,
105	testimonial, pricing, call to action.
106	
107	### 3. Draw the direction
108	
109	```bash
110	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --sector <sector> --brief "<one line about the subject>" \
111	  --sections <roles in the order of your argument> [--tone <tone>] [--have <assets>] [--keep palette,type] \
112	  --options 3
113	```
114	
115	This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory:
116	which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most
117	familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not
118	suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet:
119	
120	```bash
121	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs <the same arguments, without --options> --direction <chosen id>
122	```
123	
124	- `--sector`: `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest.
125	- `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats,
126	  pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied.
127	- `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the
128	  brief clearly asks for one.
129	- `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of
130	  the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool
131	  that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you
132	  have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill
133	  picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs
134	  is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will
135	  find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`.
136	- `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only
137	  the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles.
138	
139	The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build:
140	
141	- **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar,
142	  good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent.
143	- Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | scenes | section:<role> | direction`) only for a
144	  reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, needs an asset that does not exist,
145	  or is a section that cannot hold the real content (next point). Never redraw to get something more
146	  comfortable. Record every redraw in your report.
147	- When a dealt section cannot hold the real content (it compares three plans and there is one price;
148	  it wants five quotations and there are none), do not bend the content to fit. List the others with
149	  `--alternatives <role>`, pick the one whose assumptions match the content, and take it with
150	  `--redraw section:<role>=<id>`.
151	- **Check the palette against the subject.** A dealt palette is a set of proportions (one ground, one
152	  ink, one accent, fields) as much as a set of colours. If its colours fight the subject's own material
153	  (candy pastels for a peat whisky, neon for a mountain hut), redraw the palette once; if the subject
154	  has unmistakable colours of its own (its material, the paint of its street, the landscape outside
155	  its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so
156	  in the report.
157	- Reprint it any time with `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each
158	  section you build.
159	
160	### 4. Find the idea
161	
162	The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no
163	other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from
164	the subject itself:
165	
166	> On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**.
167	
168	Places to look for the first blank:
169	
170	- **Its output.** What does the thing produce? Put the real output on the page as material. (A camera
171	  that prints poems delivered its copy as paper slips.)
172	- **Its object or shape.** What does it physically look like, in cross-section, in silhouette?
173	  Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif.
174	- **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners?
175	- **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there?
176	- **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls?
177	- **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt,
178	  invitation, folder, manual?
179	- **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks?
180	
181	Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put
182	the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker,
183	another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a
184	loaf of bread is every bakery; the seven doors of the street this one is named after are only this one.
185	"Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea
186	was recorded as "none beyond the standard formula".
187	
188	**One live thing.** Give the page one thing the visitor can do, or that is different for each visit,
189	made from the idea: pick a wood and see the chair in it; type your name and see it cut in the
190	foundry's letters; set the loan and read the real monthly figure; see whether the hut's stove is lit
191	right now and how long until the last ferry; choose a size and see it against the room. In blind tests every winning page had one and the jurors named it first. Rules: it uses the subject's real content, it works on a phone with a thumb, it has a plain
192	fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is
193	built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9.
194	
195	**The scenes carry the idea too.** The scroll scenes on the sheet are devices waiting for a subject.
196	Decide what each one shows from your inventory before building: the fly-through passes through this
197	studio's own title cards, the route is the road this shipment really takes, the picture that opens to
198	the whole screen is the room the guest will wake up in. A scene filled with pictures that could belong
199	to anyone is a screensaver.
200	
201	### 5. Write the words
202	
203	Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`:
204	
205	- **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before
206	  committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied
207	  gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters.
208	- One supporting sentence, directly under the headline (32–48px below it) and shown with it, never
209	  docked at the foot of the first screen or held back by an animation. When the headline is a name or
210	  a figure of speech, this sentence says plainly what the thing is. One primary action, named for what
211	  it does, as a real button on the first screen.
212	- **The first screen answers the visitor's first question in large type.** For an event: what it is,
213	  when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text).
214	  For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every
215	  section the visitor came for (the line-up, the menu, the rooms, the price) has its own heading and
216	  its own place in the navigation.
217	- **Write the full content.** Every section the brief asks for delivers its information completely:
218	  the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with
219	  what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean
220	  page loses to a busier one.
221	- Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project
222	  titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm.
223	  Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics.
224	
225	### 6. Build it, still
226	
227	Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is
228	not finished. Order of work:
229	
230	1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream
231	   references tokens only. `<skill>/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token
232	   names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of
233	   its own.
234	2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big
235	   thing big and the small things small before anything else exists.
236	3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the
237	   subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,**
238	   pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a
239	   distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks.
240	4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference:
241	   1. the project's own;
242	   2. generated, if you have an image tool;
243	   3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one
244	      exists. Search them with `node <skill>/scripts/assets.mjs "<query>"` (Openverse, Wikimedia
245	      Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by
246	      default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the
247	      neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a
248	      botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the
249	      hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact
250	      section. Look at each before choosing; `--get <ref>` downloads it into `assets/` and records
251	      its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture
252	      shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room,
253	      dish, person or team;
254	   4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects,
255	      its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in
256	      the palette's real colours);
257	   5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a
258	      sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject;
259	   6. type and colour alone.

missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name).

Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to
no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and
neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop
fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the
price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by
appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at
seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where
the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on
such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that
makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list
is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6.

### 2. Write the argument

Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way
`references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any
section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features,
testimonial, pricing, call to action.

### 3. Draw the direction

```bash
node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --sector <sector> --brief "<one line about the subject>" \
  --sections <roles in the order of your argument> [--tone <tone>] [--have <assets>] [--keep palette,type] \
  --options 3
```

This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory:
which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most
familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not
suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet:

```bash
node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs <the same arguments, without --options> --direction <chosen id>
```

- `--sector`: `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest.
- `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats,
  pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied.
- `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the
  brief clearly asks for one.
- `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of
  the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool
  that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you
  have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill
  picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs
  is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will
  find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`.
- `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only
  the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles.

The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build:

- **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar,
  good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent.
- Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | scenes | section:<role> | direction`) only for a
  reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, needs an asset that does not exist,
  or is a section that cannot hold the real content (next point). Never redraw to get something more
  comfortable. Record every redraw in your report.
- When a dealt section cannot hold the real content (it compares three plans and there is one price;
  it wants five quotations and there are none), do not bend the content to fit. List the others with
  `--alternatives <role>`, pick the one whose assumptions match the content, and take it with
  `--redraw section:<role>=<id>`.
- **Check the palette against the subject.** A dealt palette is a set of proportions (one ground, one
  ink, one accent, fields) as much as a set of colours. If its colours fight the subject's own material
  (candy pastels for a peat whisky, neon for a mountain hut), redraw the palette once; if the subject
  has unmistakable colours of its own (its material, the paint of its street, the landscape outside
  its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so
  in the report.
- Reprint it any time with `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each
  section you build.

### 4. Find the idea

The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no
other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from
the subject itself:

> On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**.

Places to look for the first blank:

- **Its output.** What does the thing produce? Put the real output on the page as material. (A camera
  that prints poems delivered its copy as paper slips.)
- **Its object or shape.** What does it physically look like, in cross-section, in silhouette?
  Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif.
- **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners?
- **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there?
- **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls?
- **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt,
  invitation, folder, manual?
- **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks?

Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put
the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker,
another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a
loaf of bread is every bakery; the seven doors of the street this one is named after are only this one.
"Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea
was recorded as "none beyond the standard formula".

**One live thing.** Give the page one thing the visitor can do, or that is different for each visit,
made from the idea: pick a wood and see the chair in it; type your name and see it cut in the
foundry's letters; set the loan and read the real monthly figure; see whether the hut's stove is lit
right now and how long until the last ferry; choose a size and see it against the room. In blind tests every winning page had one and the jurors named it first. Rules: it uses the subject's real content, it works on a phone with a thumb, it has a plain
fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is
built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9.

**The scenes carry the idea too.** The scroll scenes on the sheet are devices waiting for a subject.
Decide what each one shows from your inventory before building: the fly-through passes through this
studio's own title cards, the route is the road this shipment really takes, the picture that opens to
the whole screen is the room the guest will wake up in. A scene filled with pictures that could belong
to anyone is a screensaver.

### 5. Write the words

Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`:

- **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before
  committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied
  gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters.
- One supporting sentence, directly under the headline (32–48px below it) and shown with it, never
  docked at the foot of the first screen or held back by an animation. When the headline is a name or
  a figure of speech, this sentence says plainly what the thing is. One primary action, named for what
  it does, as a real button on the first screen.
- **The first screen answers the visitor's first question in large type.** For an event: what it is,
  when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text).
  For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every
  section the visitor came for (the line-up, the menu, the rooms, the price) has its own heading and
  its own place in the navigation.
- **Write the full content.** Every section the brief asks for delivers its information completely:
  the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with
  what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean
  page loses to a busier one.
- Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project
  titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm.
  Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics.

### 6. Build it, still

Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is
not finished. Order of work:

1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream
   references tokens only. `<skill>/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token
   names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of
   its own.
2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big
   thing big and the small things small before anything else exists.
3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the
   subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,**
   pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a
   distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks.
4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference:
   1. the project's own;
   2. generated, if you have an image tool;
   3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one
      exists. Search them with `node <skill>/scripts/assets.mjs "<query>"` (Openverse, Wikimedia
      Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by
      default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the
      neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a
      botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the
      hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact
      section. Look at each before choosing; `--get <ref>` downloads it into `assets/` and records
      its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture
      shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room,
      dish, person or team;
   4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects,
      its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in
      the palette's real colours);
   5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a
      sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject;
   6. type and colour alone.

1	---
2	name: emil-design-eng
3	description: This skill encodes Emil Kowalski's philosophy on UI polish, component design, animation decisions, and the invisible details that make software feel great.
4	---
5	
6	# Design Engineering
7	
8	## Initial Response
9	
10	When this skill is first invoked without a specific question, respond only with:
11	
12	> I'm ready to help you build interfaces that feel right, my knowledge comes from Emil Kowalski's design engineering philosophy.
13	
14	Do not provide any other information until the user asks a question.
15	
16	You are a design engineer with the craft sensibility. You build interfaces where every detail compounds into something that feels right. You understand that in a world where everyone's software is good enough, taste is the differentiator.
17	
18	## Core Philosophy
19	
20	### Taste is trained, not innate
21	
22	Good taste is not personal preference. It is a trained instinct: the ability to see beyond the obvious and recognize what elevates. You develop it by surrounding yourself with great work, thinking deeply about why something feels good, and practicing relentlessly.
23	
24	When building UI, don't just make it work. Study why the best interfaces feel the way they do. Reverse engineer animations. Inspect interactions. Be curious.
25	
26	### Unseen details compound
27	
28	Most details users never consciously notice. That is the point. When a feature functions exactly as someone assumes it should, they proceed without giving it a second thought. That is the goal.
29	
30	> "All those unseen details combine to produce something that's just stunning, like a thousand barely audible voices all singing in tune." - Paul Graham
31	
32	Every decision below exists because the aggregate of invisible correctness creates interfaces people love without knowing why.
33	
34	### Beauty is leverage
35	
36	People select tools based on the overall experience, not just functionality. Good defaults and good animations are real differentiators. Beauty is underutilized in software. Use it as leverage to stand out.
37	
38	## Review Format (Required)
39	
40	When reviewing UI code, you MUST use a markdown table with Before/After columns. Do NOT use a list with "Before:" and "After:" on separate lines. Always output an actual markdown table like this:
41	
42	| Before | After | Why |
43	| --- | --- | --- |
44	| `transition: all 300ms` | `transition: transform 200ms ease-out` | Specify exact properties; avoid `all` |
45	| `transform: scale(0)` | `transform: scale(0.95); opacity: 0` | Nothing in the real world appears from nothing |
46	| `ease-in` on dropdown | `ease-out` with custom curve | `ease-in` feels sluggish; `ease-out` gives instant feedback |
47	| No `:active` state on button | `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active` | Buttons must feel responsive to press |
48	| `transform-origin: center` on popover | `transform-origin: var(--transform-origin)` | Popovers should scale from their trigger (not modals — modals stay centered) |
49	
50	Wrong format (never do this):
51	
52	```
53	Before: transition: all 300ms
54	After: transition: transform 200ms ease-out
55	────────────────────────────
56	Before: scale(0)
57	After: scale(0.95)
58	```
59	
60	Correct format: A single markdown table with | Before | After | Why | columns, one row per issue found. The "Why" column briefly explains the reasoning.
61	
62	## The Animation Decision Framework
63	
64	Before writing any animation code, answer these questions in order:
65	
66	### 1. Should this animate at all?
67	
68	**Ask:** How often will users see this animation?
69	
70	| Frequency                                                   | Decision                     |
71	| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
72	| 100+ times/day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle) | No animation. Ever.          |
73	| Tens of times/day (hover effects, list navigation)          | Remove or drastically reduce |
74	| Occasional (modals, drawers, toasts)                        | Standard animation           |
75	| Rare/first-time (onboarding, feedback forms, celebrations)  | Can add delight              |
76	
77	**Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.** These actions are repeated hundreds of times daily. Animation makes them feel slow, delayed, and disconnected from the user's actions.
78	
79	Raycast has no open/close animation. That is the optimal experience for something used hundreds of times a day.
80	
81	### 2. What is the purpose?
82	
83	Every animation must have a clear answer to "why does this animate?"
84	
85	Valid purposes:
86	
87	- **Spatial consistency**: toast enters and exits from the same direction, making swipe-to-dismiss feel intuitive
88	- **State indication**: a morphing feedback button shows the state change
89	- **Explanation**: a marketing animation that shows how a feature works
90	- **Feedback**: a button scales down on press, confirming the interface heard the user
91	- **Preventing jarring changes**: elements appearing or disappearing without transition feel broken
92	
93	If the purpose is just "it looks cool" and the user will see it often, don't animate.
94	
95	### 3. What easing should it use?
96	
97	Is the element entering or exiting?
98	  Yes → ease-out (starts fast, feels responsive)
99	  No →
100	    Is it moving/morphing on screen?
101	      Yes → ease-in-out (natural acceleration/deceleration)
102	    Is it a hover/color change?
103	      Yes → ease
104	    Is it constant motion (marquee, progress bar)?
105	      Yes → linear
106	    Default → ease-out
107	
108	**Critical: use custom easing curves.** The built-in CSS easings are too weak. They lack the punch that makes animations feel intentional.
109	
110	```css
111	/* Strong ease-out for UI interactions */
112	--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);
113	
114	/* Strong ease-in-out for on-screen movement */
115	--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1);
116	
117	/* iOS-like drawer curve (from Ionic Framework) */
118	--ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);
119	```
120	
121	**Never use ease-in for UI animations.** It starts slow, which makes the interface feel sluggish and unresponsive. A dropdown with `ease-in` at 300ms _feels_ slower than `ease-out` at the same 300ms, because ease-in delays the initial movement — the exact moment the user is watching most closely.
122	
123	**Easing curve resources:** Don't create curves from scratch. Use [easing.dev](https://easing.dev/) or [easings.co](https://easings.co/) to find stronger custom variants of standard easings.
124	
125	### 4. How fast should it be?
126	
127	| Element                  | Duration      |
128	| ------------------------ | ------------- |
129	| Button press feedback    | 100-160ms     |
130	| Tooltips, small popovers | 125-200ms     |
131	| Dropdowns, selects       | 150-250ms     |
132	| Modals, drawers          | 200-500ms     |
133	| Marketing/explanatory    | Can be longer |
134	
135	**Rule: UI animations should stay under 300ms.** A 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one. A faster-spinning spinner makes the app feel like it loads faster, even when the load time is identical.
136	
137	### Perceived performance
138	
139	Speed in animation is not just about feeling snappy — it directly affects how users perceive your app's performance:
140	
141	- A **fast-spinning spinner** makes loading feel faster (same load time, different perception)
142	- A **180ms select** animation feels more responsive than a **400ms** one
143	- **Instant tooltips** after the first one is open (skip delay + skip animation) make the whole toolbar feel faster
144	
145	The perception of speed matters as much as actual speed. Easing amplifies this: `ease-out` at 200ms _feels_ faster than `ease-in` at 200ms because the user sees immediate movement.
146	
147	## Spring Animations
148	
149	Springs feel more natural than duration-based animations because they simulate real physics. They don't have fixed durations — they settle based on physical parameters.
150	
151	### When to use springs
152	
153	- Drag interactions with momentum
154	- Elements that should feel "alive" (like Apple's Dynamic Island)
155	- Gestures that can be interrupted mid-animation
156	- Decorative mouse-tracking interactions
157	
158	### Spring-based mouse interactions
159	
160	Tying visual changes directly to mouse position feels artificial because it lacks motion. Use `useSpring` from Motion (formerly Framer Motion) to interpolate value changes with spring-like behavior instead of updating immediately.
161	
162	```jsx
163	import { useSpring } from 'framer-motion';
164	
165	// Without spring: feels artificial, instant
166	const rotation = mouseX * 0.1;
167	
168	// With spring: feels natural, has momentum
169	const springRotation = useSpring(mouseX * 0.1, {
170	  stiffness: 100,
171	  damping: 10,
172	});
173	```
174	
175	This works because the animation is **decorative** — it doesn't serve a function. If this were a functional graph in a banking app, no animation would be better. Know when decoration helps and when it hinders.
176	
177	### Spring configuration
178	
179	**Apple's approach (recommended — easier to reason about):**
180	
181	```js
182	{ type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }
183	```
184	
185	**Traditional physics (more control):**
186	
187	```js
188	{ type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }
189	```
190	
191	Keep bounce subtle (0.1-0.3) when used. Avoid bounce in most UI contexts. Use it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
192	
193	### Interruptibility advantage
194	
195	Springs maintain velocity when interrupted — CSS animations and keyframes restart from zero. This makes springs ideal for gestures users might change mid-motion. When you click an expanded item and quickly press Escape, a spring-based animation smoothly reverses from its current position.
196	
197	## Component Building Principles
198	
199	### Buttons must feel responsive
200	
201	Add `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active`. This gives instant feedback, making the UI feel like it is truly listening to the user.
202	
203	```css
204	.button {
205	  transition: transform 160ms ease-out;
206	}
207	
208	.button:active {
209	  transform: scale(0.97);
210	}
211	```
212	
213	This applies to any pressable element. The scale should be subtle (0.95-0.98).
214	
215	### Never animate from scale(0)
216	
217	Nothing in the real world disappears and reappears completely. Elements animating from `scale(0)` look like they come out of nowhere.
218	
219	Start from `scale(0.9)` or higher, combined with opacity. Even a barely-visible initial scale makes the entrance feel more natural, like a balloon that has a visible shape even when deflated.
220	
221	```css
222	/* Bad */
223	.entering {
224	  transform: scale(0);
225	}
226	
227	/* Good */
228	.entering {
229	  transform: scale(0.95);
230	  opacity: 0;
231	}
232	```
233	
234	### Make popovers origin-aware
235	
236	Popovers should scale in from their trigger, not from center. The default `transform-origin: center` is wrong for almost every popover. **Exception: modals.** Modals should keep `transform-origin: center` because they are not anchored to a specific trigger — they appear centered in the viewport.
237	
238	```css
239	/* Base UI */
240	.popover {
241	  transform-origin: var(--transform-origin);
242	}
243	```
244	
245	Whether the user notices the difference individually does not matter. In the aggregate, unseen details become visible. They compound.
246	
247	### Tooltips: skip delay on subsequent hovers
248	
249	Tooltips should delay before appearing to prevent accidental activation. But once one tooltip is open, hovering over adjacent tooltips should open them instantly with no animation. This feels faster without defeating the purpose of the initial delay.
250	
251	```css
252	.tooltip {
253	  transition: transform 125ms ease-out, opacity 125ms ease-out;
254	  transform-origin: var(--transform-origin);
255	}
256	
257	.tooltip[data-starting-style],
258	.tooltip[data-ending-style] {
259	  opacity: 0;
260	  transform: scale(0.97);
261	}
262	
263	/* Skip animation on subsequent tooltips */
264	.tooltip[data-instant] {
265	  transition-duration: 0ms;
266	}
267	```
268	
269	### Use CSS transitions over keyframes for interruptible UI
270	
271	CSS transitions can be interrupted and retargeted mid-animation. Keyframes restart from zero. For any interaction that can be triggered rapidly (adding toasts, toggling states), transitions produce smoother results.
272	
273	```css
274	/* Interruptible - good for UI */
275	.toast {
276	  transition: transform 400ms ease;
277	}
278	
279	/* Not interruptible - avoid for dynamic UI */
280	@keyframes slideIn {
281	  from {
282	    transform: translateY(100%);
283	  }
284	  to {
285	    transform: translateY(0);
286	  }
287	}
288	```
289	
290	### Use blur to mask imperfect transitions
291	
292	When a crossfade between two states feels off despite trying different easings and durations, add subtle `filter: blur(2px)` during the transition.
293	
294	**Why blur works:** Without blur, you see two distinct objects during a crossfade — the old state and the new state overlapping. This looks unnatural. Blur bridges the visual gap by blending the two states together, tricking the eye into perceiving a single smooth transformation instead of two objects swapping.
295	
296	Combine blur with scale-on-press (`scale(0.97)`) for a polished button state transition:
297	
298	```css

1	# Craft floor
2	
3	Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here except a line marked as a ban; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.
4	
5	## Verify
6	
7	Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in each batched look at the render, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.
8	
9	- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
10	- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
11	- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
12	- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
13	- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
14	- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
15	- **Browser surfaces:** the parts you did not draw still carry the design. Text selection, the caret, custom scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and the numerals in tabular data all ship with browser defaults that belong to no design system. Theme them from the palette. This is the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, and the one models skip most reliably.
16	- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
17	- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.
18	
19	## Refuse
20	
21	These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.
22	
23	Page scaffolds:
24	
25	- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
26	- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
27	- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
28	- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
29	- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.
30	
31	Surface habits:
32	
33	- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
34	- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
35	- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
36	- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
37	- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
38	- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
39	- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
40	- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
41	- Geometric masks standing in for organic contours. A circle, polygon, or radial-gradient cutout approximating a photographic subject's edge is the cheap version of the effect and reads worse than omitting it. Derive an alpha matte from the actual image, or produce a cut-out asset.
42	- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.
43	
44	The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

# Craft floor

Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here except a line marked as a ban; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.

## Verify

Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in each batched look at the render, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.

- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
- **Browser surfaces:** the parts you did not draw still carry the design. Text selection, the caret, custom scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and the numerals in tabular data all ship with browser defaults that belong to no design system. Theme them from the palette. This is the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, and the one models skip most reliably.
- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.

## Refuse

These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.

Page scaffolds:

- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.

Surface habits:

- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
- Geometric masks standing in for organic contours. A circle, polygon, or radial-gradient cutout approximating a photographic subject's edge is the cheap version of the effect and reads worse than omitting it. Derive an alpha matte from the actual image, or produce a cut-out asset.
- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.

The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

1	# iOS platform
2	
3	For native iOS / iPadOS apps: SwiftUI, UIKit, React Native, Expo, Flutter shipping to Apple hardware.
4	
5	On native, the visitor mode narrows what expression may override. HIG conformance governs structure, navigation, and interaction in every mode; brand expresses through the layer the platform leaves open (tint, type, motion, content).
6	
7	## The iOS slop test
8	
9	Would a fluent iPhone user trust this app, or pause at off-spec controls? The tell is "ported from a website": reinvented navigation bars, custom back gestures, web-shaped buttons, hover-dependent affordances. Default to the platform's components; depart only for a reason the user would thank you for.
10	
11	## Layout & structure
12	
13	- **Safe area.** Lay out inside the safe-area insets. No controls under the notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator, or rounded corners.
14	- **System navigation.** Tab bar for 2–5 top-level sections (sections, never actions), navigation stack for hierarchy, sheet for self-contained tasks. No custom global nav, no mixed metaphors.
15	- **Edge-swipe back stays alive.** The left-edge back gesture is muscle memory; never disable or overlay it.
16	- **Large titles** on top-level screens, collapsing to inline on scroll. Deep detail screens stay inline.
17	
18	## Touch targets
19	
20	- **44×44 pt minimum** for every tappable control, with breathing room between adjacent targets.
21	
22	## Typography
23	
24	- **Dynamic Type.** Use the system text styles (Large Title through Caption) so text follows the user's reading size. No hard-coded point sizes.
25	- **San Francisco carries the UI.** Body, labels, and controls stay on SF Pro / SF Compact; a brand face may appear in display moments.
26	- **11 pt floor**; Body is 17 pt.
27	
28	## Color & materials
29	
30	- **Semantic system colors** (label, secondaryLabel, systemBackground, separator, tint). They adapt to Dark Mode and increased contrast automatically; raw hex breaks there.
31	- **Dark Mode is a first-class appearance.** Design and test both.
32	- **One tint color** drives interactive elements; decoration is not its job.
33	- **System materials** for blur and translucency behind bars and sheets; no hand-rolled glassmorphism.
34	
35	## Components & controls
36	
37	- **Platform controls.** Switch, segmented control, stepper, system pickers, action sheets, alerts, context menus, swipe actions. Reinventing these for flavor is the most common native slop.
38	- **SF Symbols** for iconography: baseline-aligned, Dynamic Type-aware, weight and scale variants. Don't mix in a web icon set.
39	- **Deliberate modality.** Sheet for a focused dismissible sub-task, full-screen cover for immersion. Clear Cancel/Done; honor swipe-to-dismiss unless data loss requires a guard.
40	- **Grouped/inset lists** for settings-shaped content; no bespoke card stacks.
41	
42	## Motion
43	
44	- **System transitions.** Push slides, sheets rise, dismiss reverses the entrance. Custom transitions that fight the navigation model disorient.
45	- **Honor Reduce Motion.** Crossfade instead of parallax and large slides.
46	
47	## Verifying the build
48	
49	- **Screenshots come from the Simulator, never a browser.** Build and run, then capture with `xcrun simctl io booted screenshot <path>` (with several running, replace `booted` with the target's UDID from `xcrun simctl list devices booted`; display names can collide, the UDID never does). Capture every device class the app ships to, at least one iPhone and, when iPad is a target, one iPad, and write the files where the review flow expects them.
50	- **Dark Mode and Dynamic Type belong in the pass.** `xcrun simctl ui booted appearance dark` flips appearance, reusing the capture's UDID when several are booted; a check at a large Dynamic Type size catches the truncation a fixed layout hides.
51	- **Simulators give breadth; posture, gestures, and performance need hardware.** Say which one produced the evidence.
52

1	---
2	name: design-taste-frontend
3	description: >-
4	  tasteskill v2, the anti-slop frontend skill. Art direction for websites, distilled from a study of
5	  247 curated gallery sites (One Page Love, Awwwards Sites of the Day). Deals researched directions
6	  (idea, composition, type, palette, photographs, section blueprints) from a library, enforces a strict
7	  no-slop house style with a real-browser inspector, and runs a look-and-fix loop on screenshots. Use
8	  this whenever you build, design, redesign, restyle, polish or review a landing page, marketing site,
9	  portfolio, product page, one-pager, hero or any public-facing web page, in any stack (HTML/CSS, React,
10	  Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind) — also when the user says a page looks generic, templated,
11	  "AI-made", sloppy, or asks to make it look designed, premium, award-level or less like every other
12	  site. Also for app screens: dashboards, admin and analytics views, settings, inboxes and other screens
13	  people work in, with their own run and rules.
14	---
15	
16	# tasteskill v2
17	
18	A page built by a model usually looks like the average of every page the model has seen: a centred
19	headline over three lines, a little label above it, a row of icon cards, a soft gradient, a few thin
20	rules and a monospace caption. Nothing in it is wrong and nothing in it was decided.
21	
22	This skill replaces those defaults with decisions, in four ways:
23	
24	1. **A script deals the directions, you choose among them.** Asked to invent a look, a model picks
25	   the category default every time. `scripts/draw.mjs` deals three of twenty researched directions;
26	   you choose the one that carries the subject's idea, and the script then deals its type system,
27	   palette, hero and section compositions from a library distilled from 247 real sites.
28	2. **The idea comes from the subject.** In the study, what separated the best sites from the forgettable
29	   ones was a concept taken from the thing itself, not the styling.
30	3. **A house style with no ornaments,** measured in a real browser by `scripts/inspect.mjs`, so the
31	   rules are checked rather than hoped for.
32	4. **You look at what you made.** Screenshots at three widths, a juror's rubric, fix, look again.
33	
34	One warning learned in testing. Taking the ornaments away is only half the job; a page that has lost its
35	labels, rules and cards and gained nothing in their place reads as thin, and blind jurors rightly prefer
36	a richer page with tells over an empty page without them. The other half is substance: type set
37	larger, whole fields of colour, real pictures of this subject's world (found or drawn), and every
38	section carrying its full content. The skill is built to give you that; do not trade it for restraint.
39	
40	In the commands below `<skill>` is this skill's folder. Run them from the project's root, so the
41	working files land in `.taste-skill/` there. The scripts need Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge
42	or Chromium, and install nothing. `assets.mjs` also needs network access; it uses no API keys.
43	
44	## Page or app screen
45	
46	Decide first which of two kinds of work this is.
47	
48	- **A page** is read and scrolled: a landing page, a marketing or product site, a portfolio, an
49	  event, a restaurant, a one-pager. It follows **the run** below.
50	- **An app screen** is worked in: a dashboard, an admin or analytics view, settings, billing, an inbox
51	  or queue to work through, a wallet, a list with filters, an editor or builder. It follows
52	  **`references/app-screens.md`**: its own run, its own draw (`draw.mjs --app`), its own house rules
53	  (quiet borders, small labels and repeated panels are normal there; gradients, glows, icons in tinted
54	  squares, rainbow charts and invented vanity numbers are not) and `inspect.mjs --app`. Read that file
55	  whole before you start; the page run below does not apply.
56	
57	A product site that shows its app is a page; the interface fragments on it follow the app-screen
58	rules for their insides. Deal the product's app style once, in its own folder, with the page's colours
59	and type kept:
60	
61	```bash
62	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --app --kind <kind> --brief "<the product>" --keep palette,type --out .taste-skill/app
63	```
64	
65	and build every fragment the page shows (the hero's live screen, a feature's crop, a chart) as a real
66	piece of that app: `assets/app.css` for its panels, tables and controls, `assets/charts.js` for its
67	charts, real data that adds up, one finding stated, cropped and scaled the way the page's blueprint
68	treats a picture. A fragment that looks like a working product is the strongest picture a software page
69	has; grey bars and lorem numbers are the weakest. When a request mixes both (a landing page and the
70	dashboard behind it), build each with its own run and one shared palette and typeface.
71	
72	## The run
73	
74	Do these in order. Steps 1–5 take a few minutes and decide whether the page is any good.
75	
76	### 1. Read the brief and the project
77	
78	Find out what is real: the subject, the audience, the one thing the page must get someone to do, the
79	stack, any existing brand (colours, fonts, logo), and above all **what imagery truly exists**: the
80	project's own photographs or product shots, a real interface that can be shown, an image generation
81	tool you can call, or nothing. Do not plan around pictures you do not have. Nothing of its own is
82	rarely nothing at all: the subject's city, street, materials and history are in open archives and
83	museums, free to use with a credit (step 6, `scripts/assets.mjs`).
84	
85	If the request is vague, decide and state your reading in one line instead of asking. Ask only when a
86	missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name).
87	
88	Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to
89	no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and
90	neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop
91	fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the
92	price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by
93	appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at
94	seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where
95	the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on
96	such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that
97	makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list
98	is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6.
99	
100	### 2. Write the argument
101	
102	Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way
103	`references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any
104	section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features,
105	testimonial, pricing, call to action.
106	
107	### 3. Draw the direction
108	
109	```bash
110	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --sector <sector> --brief "<one line about the subject>" \
111	  --sections <roles in the order of your argument> [--tone <tone>] [--have <assets>] [--keep palette,type] \
112	  --options 3
113	```
114	
115	This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory:
116	which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most
117	familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not
118	suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet:
119	
120	```bash
121	node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs <the same arguments, without --options> --direction <chosen id>
122	```
123	
124	- `--sector`: `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest.
125	- `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats,
126	  pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied.
127	- `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the
128	  brief clearly asks for one.
129	- `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of
130	  the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool
131	  that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you
132	  have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill
133	  picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs
134	  is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will
135	  find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`.
136	- `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only
137	  the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles.
138	
139	The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build:
140	
141	- **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar,
142	  good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent.
143	- Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | scenes | section:<role> | direction`) only for a
144	  reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, needs an asset that does not exist,
145	  or is a section that cannot hold the real content (next point). Never redraw to get something more
146	  comfortable. Record every redraw in your report.
147	- When a dealt section cannot hold the real content (it compares three plans and there is one price;
148	  it wants five quotations and there are none), do not bend the content to fit. List the others with
149	  `--alternatives <role>`, pick the one whose assumptions match the content, and take it with
150	  `--redraw section:<role>=<id>`.
151	- **Check the palette against the subject.** A dealt palette is a set of proportions (one ground, one
152	  ink, one accent, fields) as much as a set of colours. If its colours fight the subject's own material
153	  (candy pastels for a peat whisky, neon for a mountain hut), redraw the palette once; if the subject
154	  has unmistakable colours of its own (its material, the paint of its street, the landscape outside
155	  its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so
156	  in the report.
157	- Reprint it any time with `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each
158	  section you build.
159	
160	### 4. Find the idea
161	
162	The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no
163	other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from
164	the subject itself:
165	
166	> On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**.
167	
168	Places to look for the first blank:
169	
170	- **Its output.** What does the thing produce? Put the real output on the page as material. (A camera
171	  that prints poems delivered its copy as paper slips.)
172	- **Its object or shape.** What does it physically look like, in cross-section, in silhouette?
173	  Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif.
174	- **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners?
175	- **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there?
176	- **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls?
177	- **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt,
178	  invitation, folder, manual?
179	- **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks?
180	
181	Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put
182	the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker,
183	another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a
184	loaf of bread is every bakery; the seven doors of the street this one is named after are only this one.
185	"Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea
186	was recorded as "none beyond the standard formula".
187	
188	**One live thing.** Give the page one thing the visitor can do, or that is different for each visit,
189	made from the idea: pick a wood and see the chair in it; type your name and see it cut in the
190	foundry's letters; set the loan and read the real monthly figure; see whether the hut's stove is lit
191	right now and how long until the last ferry; choose a size and see it against the room. In blind tests every winning page had one and the jurors named it first. Rules: it uses the subject's real content, it works on a phone with a thumb, it has a plain
192	fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is
193	built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9.
194	
195	**The scenes carry the idea too.** The scroll scenes on the sheet are devices waiting for a subject.
196	Decide what each one shows from your inventory before building: the fly-through passes through this
197	studio's own title cards, the route is the road this shipment really takes, the picture that opens to
198	the whole screen is the room the guest will wake up in. A scene filled with pictures that could belong
199	to anyone is a screensaver.
200	
201	### 5. Write the words
202	
203	Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`:
204	
205	- **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before
206	  committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied
207	  gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters.
208	- One supporting sentence, directly under the headline (32–48px below it) and shown with it, never
209	  docked at the foot of the first screen or held back by an animation. When the headline is a name or
210	  a figure of speech, this sentence says plainly what the thing is. One primary action, named for what
211	  it does, as a real button on the first screen.
212	- **The first screen answers the visitor's first question in large type.** For an event: what it is,
213	  when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text).
214	  For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every
215	  section the visitor came for (the line-up, the menu, the rooms, the price) has its own heading and
216	  its own place in the navigation.
217	- **Write the full content.** Every section the brief asks for delivers its information completely:
218	  the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with
219	  what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean
220	  page loses to a busier one.
221	- Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project
222	  titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm.
223	  Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics.
224	
225	### 6. Build it, still
226	
227	Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is
228	not finished. Order of work:
229	
230	1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream
231	   references tokens only. `<skill>/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token
232	   names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of
233	   its own.
234	2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big
235	   thing big and the small things small before anything else exists.
236	3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the
237	   subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,**
238	   pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a
239	   distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks.
240	4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference:
241	   1. the project's own;
242	   2. generated, if you have an image tool;
243	   3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one
244	      exists. Search them with `node <skill>/scripts/assets.mjs "<query>"` (Openverse, Wikimedia
245	      Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by
246	      default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the
247	      neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a
248	      botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the
249	      hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact
250	      section. Look at each before choosing; `--get <ref>` downloads it into `assets/` and records
251	      its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture
252	      shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room,
253	      dish, person or team;
254	   4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects,
255	      its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in
256	      the palette's real colours);
257	   5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a
258	      sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject;
259	   6. type and colour alone.
